content.body: Finding two numbers that add up to a target is a common puzzle. Today, we'll solve it efficiently for a sorted array. You'll learn to use a clever memory trick to avoid checking every possible pair.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
1. Explain why a brute-force approach becomes inefficient for large arrays.
2. Implement a single-pass solution using a lookup structure (object or Map).
3. Determine what to store as keys and values in your lookup.
4. Decide when to check the lookup versus when to add to it.
5. Return the correct indices for the Two Sum II problem.
content.title: What you'll learn
One more
content.successMessage: Great! You checked pairs until you found 7 and 8 (or 9 and 6, etc.).

content.body: What you just did was brute force: you picked each element from the start and added it with others until you found the pair. That works for small arrays.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When the array has 10,000 numbers, checking every pair is too slow. We need a better method. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Remember what we have already seen. Instead of re-scanning the array, we can use a lookup structure (like an object or Map) to note numbers we've encountered. This way, we can check in one step if the number we need has been seen before.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: A notebook where we write down what we've seen and check it in one step.

content.body: We'll use a single pass and a lookup structure. For each number, we calculate what other number we need to reach the target. We check our 'notebook' to see if we've already seen that needed number. If yes, we found our pair! If not, we write down the current number and move on.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
Walkthrough with [2, 7, 11, 15], target 9:
1. Check 2 → need 7? Not in notebook. Add 2 to notebook.
2. Check 7 → need 2? Yes, 2 is in notebook (from index 0). Return [0, 1].

Key vs. value: We store the number as the key and its index as the value.
When to check vs. add: Check for the needed number first; if not found, then add the current number.

content.body:
1. Create an empty object (or Map) to act as our lookup notebook.
2. Loop through each number in the array.
3. For the current number, calculate: needed = target - currentNumber.
4. Check if 'needed' is already in our notebook.
   - If YES, return the indices: [index of needed, current index].
   - If NO, add the current number and its index to the notebook.
5. Continue until a pair is found.
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up the function
steps.instruction: Create a function called twoSum that takes two parameters: numbers (a sorted array) and target (a number). Return an array of two indices.
steps.hint: Follow the standard function syntax. We'll fill in the logic later.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named twoSum with parameters numbers and target.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! The function structure is ready.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the function is named twoSum and takes two parameters.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. We need a function named twoSum that accepts numbers and target.

steps.title: Create the lookup notebook
steps.instruction: Inside the function, create a variable called seen and set it to an empty object. This will store numbers we've already encountered.
steps.hint: Use let or const to declare the variable.
steps.expectedOutcome: A variable named seen initialized to an empty object {}.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! The notebook is ready to remember seen numbers.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. Declare a variable named seen and set it to an empty object.

steps.title: Loop through the array
steps.instruction: Add a for loop to iterate through each element in the numbers array. Use index i to track the current position.
steps.hint: Standard for loop: for (let i = 0; i < numbers.length; i++)
steps.expectedOutcome: A for loop that iterates through indices of the numbers array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! The loop will go through each number one by one.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check the loop syntax. We need to iterate from 0 to numbers.length.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's set up the loop: for (let i = 0; i < numbers.length; i++)

steps.title: Calculate needed and check the notebook
steps.instruction: Inside the loop, calculate the needed number: target - numbers[i]. Then check if needed is already a key in the seen object. If it is, return an array with the index from seen[needed] and the current index i.
steps.hint: Use an if statement to check if seen[needed] is not undefined.
steps.expectedOutcome: Code that calculates needed, checks the lookup, and returns indices if found.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You're checking the notebook before adding anything.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Calculate needed, then check if seen[needed] exists.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try: let needed = target - numbers[i]; if (seen[needed] !== undefined) return [seen[needed], i];

steps.title: Add current number to the notebook
steps.instruction: If the needed number was not found in seen, add the current number to the notebook. Store it as a key with its index i as the value.
steps.hint: After the if check, add seen[numbers[i]] = i;
steps.expectedOutcome: Code that adds the current number and index to the seen object when needed is not found.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! Now the notebook remembers each number after we check it.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. After the if block, store the current number in seen.
steps.feedbackWrong: Add: seen[numbers[i]] = i; This writes the number into our notebook.

content.body: Congratulations! You've implemented an efficient solution for Two Sum II using a hashmap. Remember: the key idea is to 'remember what we have already seen' using a lookup structure. You store the number as the key and its index as the value. Always check the lookup first; if the needed number isn't there, then add the current number. This single-pass approach works beautifully for sorted and unsorted arrays alike.
